title: Red-Wine Gravy
subtitle: Built on the roast pan drippings
excerpt: A proper Sunday roast gravy made from the roasting tin drippings, deglazed with red wine, thickened with flour, and finished with stock. Rich, deep, and full of the flavour from the roast.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pan gravy is one of the oldest principles of British cookery: the flavour left in the roasting tin after cooking a joint is too valuable to discard. The technique of deglazing the browned sediment (the fond) with liquid to make a sauce appears in some form in virtually every cookery tradition. In British roasting, the addition of flour to the fat creates a roux that thickens the gravy as the liquid is added, producing a well-bodied sauce rather than a thin jus. Red wine adds depth and acidity; stock adds body. The quality of the gravy depends almost entirely on the quality of the roasting juices and the stock.

content.text: Pour away any excess fat from the roasting tin, leaving only 1 to 2 tablespoons of the drippings and any browned sediment. Place the tin directly on the hob over medium heat: do not clean the tin. The browned residue on the base is where all the flavour lives. Work quickly when adding the wine so it reduces while the tin is still very hot.

items.preparation: stirred into the roasting tin drippings

content.text: Pour away all but about 2 tablespoons of the fat from the roasting tin. Place the tin over medium heat on the hob. Sprinkle in the flour and stir vigorously with a wooden spoon, scraping up all the browned bits from the base. Cook for 1 to 2 minutes, stirring constantly.

Pour in the red wine and stir hard to incorporate: the liquid will splutter and steam. Let it bubble for 1 minute to cook off the alcohol. Gradually add the stock, stirring all the time, until the gravy is smooth.

Simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until the gravy has reduced to a good pouring consistency. Add the Worcestershire sauce, taste, and season with salt and pepper. Strain through a sieve into a warm jug if a very smooth gravy is wanted.
